solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Be proud and resolute going outside (5,3)

indicatorNotes.going outside: STOUT goes round the outside of AND

blocks.note: stout = resolute, as in a stout defence
the word itself, taken as printed

annotation.surface: Advice to stand tall and firm when you step out into the world.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Proud' here is the physical sense, sticking out from a surface, as a nail stands proud of the wood; 'and', which looks like a joining word, is the letters placed inside.
annotation.definitionFit: Something that is proud projects beyond its surroundings, which is exactly what it does when it stands out.

entries.clue: Perhaps May article on Salvation Army (7)

indicatorNotes.Perhaps: perhaps marks the definition as one example of a wider class, here a first name that one famous May carried

blocks.note: the usual initials for the Salvation Army

annotation.surface: Someone asks whether May will see an article written about the Salvation Army.
annotation.walkthrough: May looks like the month, or a verb of permission; it is the surname of Theresa May, the former British prime minister.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: May is the surname of one famous bearer of the first name, the former British prime minister (2016-2019).

entries.clue: Girl raised grouse on island (5)

indicatorNotes.raised: in a down clue, raising a word writes it bottom to top

blocks.note: to grouse is to moan, complain

annotation.surface: A girl kicks up a fuss about something while stuck on an island.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Grouse' looks like the game bird, which fits an island scene, but it is the verb meaning complain.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the answer is a girl's first name, Hebrew in origin and borne by Ruth's mother-in-law in the Bible.

entries.clue: No spring chicken daring to go topless (3)

indicatorNotes.to go topless: in a down clue the top of the word is its first letter, which is removed

blocks.note: BOLD without its first letter B

annotation.surface: An older woman shows some daring by going topless.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a daring older sunbather, and the definition is the idiom for someone past their youth.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone who is no spring chicken is no longer young, that is old.

entries.clue: Check striker fit for international? (4,5)

blocks.note: a match is struck to light it, so it is a striker

annotation.surface: A manager checks whether the centre forward is fit enough to play for his country.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Striker' pretends to be a footballer; it is a match. A test match is an international cricket or rugby game.
annotation.definitionFit: A Test match is a game between two national sides, so it is an international.

entries.clue: Play involving black fellow (4)

indicatorNotes.involving: TOY involves, that is takes in, B

blocks.note: to play with something is to toy with it

annotation.surface: A drama whose plot centres on a black man.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Play' looks like a noun, a drama, but it is the verb toy. Crossword fellows are often any man's name.
annotation.definitionFit: Toby is a man's name, and a fellow is a man.

entries.clue: Fish sandwiches to present without thought (4,3)

indicatorNotes.sandwiches: TROUT holds TO between its slices

blocks.note: the word itself, taken as printed

annotation.surface: A fish sandwich handed over without a second's thought.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sandwiches' fits the lunch picture but is a verb here, meaning puts between.
annotation.definitionFit: To trot out an excuse is to offer a stock one without thinking.

entries.clue: Intolerant sort to leave in short while (5)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' places the word before it inside the one after, so the leaving sits in the short while

blocks.note: wait a bit = wait a short while

annotation.surface: Someone narrow-minded is told to clear off for a little while.
annotation.walkthrough: A bit of time is a short while, as in back in a bit.
annotation.definitionFit: A bigot is a person intolerant of other views or groups.

entries.clue: Leading character is somewhat lecherous (4)

indicatorNotes.somewhat: only some of the next word is used

blocks.note: the letters sit inside this word, after its first three and before its last two

annotation.surface: The star of the story turns out to be a bit of a lech.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a verdict on a character; lec(HERO)us holds the answer inside the one long word.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the protagonist, the leading character, of a story, film or play.

entries.clue: Drive away duck circling one small lake (8)

indicatorNotes.circling: DODGE goes round the other letters

blocks.note: to duck a blow is to dodge it
S = small, as on clothing labels

annotation.surface: Chasing off a duck that keeps paddling round a pond.
annotation.walkthrough: The duck looks like the bird to be driven off; it is the verb meaning dodge, split D…ODGE round I, S and L.
annotation.definitionFit: To dislodge something is to force it out of place, driving it away.

entries.clue: Welsh aim wrecked in London borough (8)

indicatorNotes.wrecked: the letters are wrecked and rebuilt

annotation.surface: A Welshman's plans come to grief on a trip to London.
annotation.walkthrough: Lewisham is a borough of south-east London; the clue sets Wales against London to hide it.
annotation.definitionFit: Lewisham is one of the thirty-two London boroughs.

entries.clue: Six-footer encountered in verse? (9)

blocks.note: the surface reads a very tall person; in prosody a foot is a unit of rhythm, so this is something six feet long
the question mark admits the pun: this six-footer is met in poetry, not on a basketball court

annotation.surface: A very tall person turns up in a poem.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Six-footer' suggests a tall person; in poetry a foot is a unit of rhythm, and a line of six feet is a hexameter.
annotation.definitionFit: A hexameter is a line of verse made up of six metrical feet.

entries.clue: Too much love for German fellow (4)

blocks.note: OTT = over the top, too much

annotation.surface: A German man is said to be excessively in love.
annotation.walkthrough: OTT is British slang for over the top, overdone.
annotation.definitionFit: Otto is a typical German man's name.

entries.clue: Organ swell that might hamper listener? (6)

blocks.note: the ear is an organ of the body

annotation.surface: A church organ's swell pedal gets in the way of someone trying to listen.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Organ swell' reads as the musical instrument's volume control; the organ is the ear and swell is wax, as a growing moon waxes.
annotation.definitionFit: A build-up of earwax blocks the ear and dulls a listener's hearing.
annotation.definitionNote: the definition is a descriptive phrase, standing for a thing that might hamper a listener

entries.clue: Material from most evil news boss (7)

blocks.note: the worst is the most evil
ED = editor, the boss of a newspaper

annotation.surface: A scoop sourced from a thoroughly wicked newspaper editor.
annotation.walkthrough: Worsted is a smooth woollen cloth, used for suits.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the answer is a smooth woollen cloth named after Worstead in Norfolk, one kind of material.

entries.clue: Shows disapproval about our heartless lecturers (6)

indicatorNotes.about: TUTS goes about the other letters
indicatorNotes.heartless: OUR loses its middle letter U

blocks.note: to tut is to click the tongue in disapproval

annotation.surface: Students click their tongues at their spineless teachers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Our' looks like a possessive attaching to the lecturers; it is fodder that loses its heart.
annotation.definitionFit: University tutors teach and lecture students.

entries.clue: Go berserk in high-scoring Lord’s game? (3,4)

blocks.note: to go wild, lose all restraint; an idiom with a verb, in 3,4
Lord's is the London cricket ground; in a high-scoring match the runs come riotously

annotation.surface: A cricketer loses his temper during a big-hitting match at Lord's.
annotation.walkthrough: Lord's is the London cricket ground; the question mark flags the playful reading of RUN RIOT, where runs are what go wild.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom twice over: to go wild without restraint, and, read literally, a game in which runs pile up riotously.

entries.clue: Addict from southeast in ancient city (4)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' places the compass point inside the city, as if the south-east quarter lay within its walls

blocks.note: Ur, the Sumerian city, is crosswords' favourite ancient city

annotation.surface: An addict hails from the south-east corner of an old city.
annotation.walkthrough: A user is a drug user, hence an addict.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the drugs sense: someone who takes drugs habitually is described by the shorter word.

entries.clue: Sell battered fish over time (5)

indicatorNotes.battered: FISH is battered out of shape
indicatorNotes.over: in a down clue, the fish sits over the T

annotation.surface: A chip shop takes a long time to sell its battered fish.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Battered' fits the chip-shop picture but means knocked about, rearranged. To shift stock is trade slang for selling it.
annotation.definitionFit: Shops that shift goods sell them, moving them off the shelves.

entries.clue: Wood in stacks sheltering a pig (8)

indicatorNotes.sheltering: MANY shelters A HOG inside it

annotation.surface: A pig takes cover among piles of logs in the woods.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stacks' looks like woodpiles, fitting the scene; it means lots, many.
annotation.definitionFit: Mahogany is a hard reddish-brown wood.

entries.clue: Italian city an ego destroyed (5)

indicatorNotes.destroyed: the letters are knocked apart and rebuilt

annotation.surface: A visit to an Italian city crushes someone's self-importance.
annotation.walkthrough: The Italian city is Genoa, the northern port.
annotation.definitionFit: Genoa is a port city in north-west Italy.

entries.clue: Tyrant adroit manoeuvring around court (8)

indicatorNotes.manoeuvring: the letters of ADROIT are manoeuvred into a new order
indicatorNotes.around: the rearranged letters go around CT

annotation.surface: A despot skilfully plots his moves around the royal court.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Manoeuvring' reads as political scheming, fitting a tyrant at court; it is the instruction to rearrange ADROIT.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an absolute ruler who holds unchecked power, as tyrants do.

entries.clue: Strange Caribbean spirit (3)

blocks.note: old-fashioned British slang for odd or peculiar, as in 'a ___ do'
the spirit is the drink, distilled from sugar cane across the Caribbean

annotation.surface: A ghostly presence haunts a Caribbean island.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spirit' suggests a ghost, which fits 'Strange'; it is the drink. RUM meaning odd is old-fashioned British slang, as in a rum do.
annotation.definitionFit: Rum is both an odd thing and a spirit made from sugar cane in the Caribbean.

entries.clue: Turned on by Irish film genre (4)

indicatorNotes.Turned: something turned faces the other way, so the word after it is written back to front

annotation.surface: Someone finds an Irish crime movie thrilling.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turned on' reads as a phrase meaning excited; split it and 'Turned' works on 'on' alone.
annotation.definitionFit: Noir, short for film noir, is a genre of dark crime films.

entries.clue: Boss in educational activity mostly (4)

indicatorNotes.mostly: most of the word is kept, dropping its last letter

blocks.note: STUDY without its last letter Y

annotation.surface: The head teacher sits in on a lesson for most of it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Boss' looks like a manager; it is a raised knob or stud, as on a shield.
annotation.definitionFit: A boss is a round raised ornament, the same thing as a stud.

entries.clue: Force breaches defences (8)

blocks.note: to ram is to force, drive through

annotation.surface: An army smashes through a castle's defences.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as one battle report, so 'breaches' looks like the verb of the sentence; it is a second piece of wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Ramparts are defensive walls, the defences of a fort.
